chunks: "Typically I'd describe a surface-mount line first, in order. The bare board comes in and gets loaded.
A stencil printer squeegees solder paste onto the pads through a metal stencil.
Many lines then have solder-paste inspection, a 3D check that the paste volume and position are right, because most solder defects start at the printer.
Next, pick-and-place machines take parts from tape reels and trays and drop them on the paste, using cameras to align to the board's fiducials.
The board then travels through a reflow oven, which follows a temperature profile that dries the flux, melts the solder and cools it into joints.
After reflow, automated optical inspection looks for missing, shifted, tombstoned or bridged parts. For a double-sided board you flip it and repeat for the second side.
Through-hole parts, like connectors and big electrolytics, are inserted and soldered by wave, selective soldering or by hand.
Then the board goes to test: in-circuit test or flying probe for opens, shorts and component values, and then a functional test that powers it up and exercises it.
Finally there can be cleaning, programming of firmware, conformal coating and depaneling.
The principle is to catch defects as early as you can, since fixing a bad joint at the printer costs almost nothing and finding it after the box is sealed costs a lot."
